nh_cliff_boulders.blurb: A cluster of granite boulders inside Pawtuckaway State Park in Nottingham, found by walking up and left above the Lower Slabs. Roughly thirty boulder problems cover the full range, from V0 warm-ups through a solid middle band of V3 to V7 and into a handful of very hard lines at V9 to V11. It makes a good stop for projecting or for loosening up before heading to the busier boulders nearby, and it tends to stay quiet when those fill up. Expect the coarse, skin-wearing granite typical of the park, and plan for bugs in late spring and early summer.

nh_eagle_cliff.blurb: An alpine-feeling cliff high above Franconia Notch, part of Hounds Hump Ridge and reached by a long uphill walk. The Main Wall holds most of the routes, with a few more on smaller flanks. Climbing is mostly traditional and alpine-style, with a few bolted sport lines, and the grades run from 5.8 to the low 5.13s with most routes between 5.10 and 5.12. Views take in the notch and the big cliff across from it. The wall faces southwest, catches sun through much of the day and dries fast, though weather up here can turn quickly and loose rock turns up in places. Crowds are rare compared with the roadside crags.

nh_jimmy_cliff.blurb: Two neighboring schist walls high on Rattlesnake Mountain at Rumney, which keeps them drier than many of the lower crags. About twenty-eight routes, mostly bolted with some trad, run from 5.3 up to the low 5.12s, with plenty of easy and moderate lines packed close together and a few two-pitch slabs. That makes it a favorite for beginners, guided groups and anyone learning to lead. A breeze and partial to full sun make it a decent choice after rain, but it can get crowded when parties spill up from below. Choose the left or right side at a fork in the trail.

nh_mordor_wall_the.blurb: A steep, intimidating granite wall on Cathedral Ledge above North Conway, with Thin Air Face to its left and the Cathedral Cave to its right. It is best known for big-wall style aid climbing, with a smaller set of hard, committing free routes; most free lines sit around 5.11 to 5.12, and a few are harder still. Roughly two dozen lines in all, mostly traditional, plus a handful of aid routes. The wall is gently overhanging and the rock is blank in places, so it suits experienced parties comfortable with serious pitches. In rare big-ice winters it has even seen ice and mixed ascents.

nh_table_mountain.blurb: A south-facing granite slab, 200 to 300 feet tall, tucked off Bear Notch Road between the Kancamagus Highway and Bartlett. About two dozen traditional routes, many of them two pitches, are mostly 5.4 to 5.9 with a few 5.10s, so it suits moderate leaders looking for solitude. Bolts were mostly replaced with modern ones, but cruxes are usually protected better than the easier ground between them, and runouts can be serious. The hike in takes close to an hour, and the descent is by rappel. It sees few visitors even on busy weekends.
nh_table_mountain.approach: Hike the Attitash trail from the east side of Bear Notch Road; allow roughly an hour or a little less.

nh_warmup_area.blurb: A small group of five granite boulders in Blair Woods at Pawtuckaway State Park, and the spot where most boulderers begin their day. About twenty-five problems range from V0 to V9, with a good helping of easy and moderate lines, a few mid-range problems and several tougher classics. Many topouts are sloping, so commit to your feet. The boulders sit furthest along the trail loop from the entrance, a short walk from the parking lot. Granite here is rough on skin, and the woods are buggy in late spring and early summer.
nh_warmup_area.parking_note: Take Route 156 to Deerfield Road, go left where a sign points to the boat launch, and drive on to the parking area. Keep off the road shoulders and out of the trailer spaces.
